new_statements.quote: The language has been described under two sections, viz., phonology and grammar. The present chapter deals with the phonology. At the phonological level, the segmental and suprasegmental features, which display meaning differentiating function in words, have been presented. [...] The suprasegmental features of stress and tone do not have any functional roles to play in Saurashtri. Besides the set of oral vowels a few nasal vowels (of limited occurrence) are noticed. Length in vowels is found to be phonemic in certain environments and non-phonemic in others.
new_statements.citation: Ramasubramanian, K. S. 1968 [Glottolog: 1969]. A linguistic study of Saurashtri language. Ph.D. thesis, University of Poona (Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute), Chapter 2 'Phonology'.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, p. 14 (opening section, second paragraph)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the held page image (Shodhganga scan of Ramasubramanian 1968, Chapter 2 'Phonology', printed p. 14, footer ': - 14 - :') and read it directly: the second paragraph reads exactly 'The suprasegmental features of stress and tone do not have any functional roles to play in Saurashtri. Besides the set of oral vowels a few nasal vowels ( of limited occurrence) are noticed. Length in vowels is found to be phonemic in certain environments and non-phonemic in others.' The opening sentences quoted before the '[...]' are also verbatim (the ellipsis skips one sentence about words as pause-isolable units). The contents page  confirms phonology is confined to ch. 2 (pp. 14-117; ch. 3 Grammar, then…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (and tone) are stated to be non-functional, i.e. not contrastive, in Madurai Saurashtri; the thesis gives no rule for where phonetic prominence falls, and the 104-page phonology chapter contains no further discussion of stress. The 2023 LSI Tamil Nadu chapter (Vedamanickam, p. 800) independently repeats that 'tone, stress and accent are not distinctive features in this language', again without a placement rule. No opened source states a stress position.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of spoken Madurai Saurashtri (words defined as units isolable by pauses); statement concerns phonemic function only, not phonetic placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Ramasubramanian 1968 describes Saurashtri 'as it is spoken today at Madurai' (fieldwork at Madurai, informants there) = the Southern/Madurai variety of saur1248; LSI 2023 also centres on Madurai district. Učida 1991 (wishlist) describes the Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh) variety. Grierson's 'Paṭṇūlī/Saurāshṭrī' and Joshi's 'Khatri dialect' refer to the same silk-weaver community's speech (Khatri = the Deccan/Bombay-side name). All fall under glottocode saur1248 (no Glottolog sub-dialect codes).

sources.citation: Vedamanickam, P. Edward. 2023. Saurashtra/Saurashtri. In: Linguistic Survey of India: Tamil Nadu, pp. 784-849. Kolkata: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India.
sources.note: Sec. 2.7 'Suprasegmental Feature', printed p. 800 (PDF p. 819): 'Apart from segmental phonemes Saurashtra make suprasegmental distinctions in tone and nasality. Suprasegmentals include tone, stress, and prosody. Tone, stress and accent are not distinctive features in this language.' Only length is exemplified; no placement rule. The wording is boilerplate repeated in the Kathodi and Urali chapters of the same volume.
